newsitem.title: JAPAN: State Street says Japan stocks a buy.
newsitem.headline: State Street says Japan stocks a buy.

text.p: Japanese stocks are now a buy for offshore pension funds in the view of State Street Corp, a U.S. fund management and custodial firm.

"The financial sector obviously has some issues," William Hunt, president of State Street's Tokyo-based trust banking subsidiary said in an interview. "But overall, as a market, Japan is relatively attractive."
State Street manages about $10 billion in global pension funds invested in Japanese markets. The company's overall assets under management total $320 billion.

On average, over the past 10 years, State Street has been able to generate average returns of six percentage points above the TOPIX index of first section shares in Japan by following a strict quantitative approach, Hunt said.
Those same models now suggest that valuations have returned to levels not seen since the bubble era of inflated asset prices of the late 1980s and early 1990s.
"Japan is relatively cheap," said Isao Kamatsuka, vice-president and head of asset management in Tokyo.

Kamatsuka said the average price-to-book ratio of first section shares on the Tokyo Stock Exchange is down to just 1.99 now, compared with an average of 2.64 over the past five years and 3.5 for U.S. shares.
Price to cash-flow ratios and earnings growth projections also suggest that Japanese shares are a buy, Kamatsuka said.
"We also don't agree with the view that the economy is dwindling down," he said. "We think this is a typical recovery."
State Street favours "capital-investment related" shares, such as Japanese machine tool makers, and is shunning financial issues, including banks.
State Street Trust and Banking also manages $2.5 billion equivalent on behalf of Japanese pension funds, much of that in global equities and index funds.

Assets under management in Japan have jumped from about $25 million two years ago in part because the easing of a rule last February that had imposed a ceiling on corporate pension accounts investment in offshore markets, Hunt said.
Now the proposed "Big Bang" deregulation of Japan's financial markets could see the mutual fund business boom here, he said.
"Once banks are able to distribute (mutual funds) we expect there's going to be an explosion," he said.
